title: Short Stuff: Bengal Cats
summary: Short Stuff episode on Bengal cats. The hosts explain that the Bengal is a hybrid breed descended from the Asian leopard cat (a small wild cat of southern and eastern Asia) crossed with domestic cats. They trace the feline lineage back about six million years, describe leopard-cat size and rosette spots, and recount the breed's origins: Willard Centerwall's 1971 feline leukemia research at Loma Linda University, conservationist Jean Mill's breeding program aimed at reducing demand for leopard skin coats, and breeder Bill Engler, who had a leopard cat named Shah and whose name is not the source of the breed name. They cover coat colors and patterns (including snow leopard-like coats), the cats' athleticism, water-loving habits, high energy and demanding temperament, prices, state laws restricting ownership or breeding, and the hosts' disapproval of buying hybrid cats from pet stores. The episode closes with a tangent about a Chihuahua with a non-retractable tongue and a dog breed often called ugly.

segments.title: Opening banter
segments.summary: Josh welcomes listeners to Short Stuff and introduces the Bengal cat episode.

segments.title: Bengal cat as leopard-house cat hybrid
segments.summary: The hosts explain that the Bengal cat is a cross between a house cat and the small wild Asian leopard cat, which is not related to the leopard.

segments.title: Feline lineage and rosettes
segments.summary: Chuck describes the split of cat lineages about six million years ago, the house cat (Felis catus) and the leopard cat, and the leopard cat's size and habitat. Josh explains rosettes.

segments.title: Willard Centerwall and Jean Mill
segments.summary: Willard Centerwall started hybridizing cats in 1971 while at Loma Linda University, researching feline leukemia resistance. Breeder Jean Mill collaborated with him; as a conservationist she hoped leopard-looking pets would reduce demand for leopard skin coats and aid wild leopard conservation.

segments.title: Bill Engler and the breed name
segments.summary: Chuck describes breeder Bill Engler, a zoo keeper and animal importer whose leopard cat named Shah was involved in early Bengal kittens. The hosts say the breed name comes from the Asian leopard cat's name, not from Engler's name.

segments.title: Bengal appearance, coat colors, and build
segments.summary: The hosts describe rosette shapes, marble coats, coat colors up to white and snow leopard-like coats, and the cats' muscular, athletic build and taller hind legs.

segments.title: Bengal temperament, care demands, and prices
segments.summary: The cats are energetic, enjoy water and walks, and need much more stimulation than average cats. Buyers are often unprepared. Snow leopard-style kittens can sell for about two thousand dollars. Chuck notes that wild ancestry means more socialization is needed, and that several states restrict ownership or breeding, with a how-stuff-works article mentioned as the source.

segments.title: Pet store signs and adoption
segments.summary: The hosts criticize permanent pet-store signs advertising kittens and puppies, distinguishing them from adoption events, and recall seeing a pet store with special-needs dogs.

segments.title: Chihuahua tongue and ugliest dog tangent
segments.summary: Josh recalls a Chihuahua that could not retract its tongue. Chuck mentions a dog breed often called the ugliest and suggests a future short on it.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts end the episode, followed by the iHeartRadio production credit.
